extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for public relations counselors on advising clients, shaping and responding to public opinion, and using media channels strategically and ethically. Covers diagnosis of public beliefs, channel selection, message tactics, and interaction with the press and other institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary function of public relations counsel (proactive advisory role)
rubrics_metrics.description: The counsel's primary function is not merely to bring clients to public attention or extricate them from difficulties, but to advise clients how positive results can be accomplished in public relations and to keep them from drifting into unfortunate or harmful situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advise on strategy and preventive policy changes rather than only reactive publicity. Counsel must proactively recommend modifications in policy in accordance with changes in public point of view; avoid waiting for crises to act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous monitoring of events and public sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations counsel must 'be alive to the events of the day — not only the events that are printed but the events which are forming hour by hour, as reported in the words that are spoken on the street, in the smoking cars, in the school room, or expressed in any of the other forms of thought communication that make up public opinion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor both formal media reporting and informal conversational channels; gather real-time signals from diverse social settings to detect shifts in opinion early; include street-level, institutional, and interpersonal feedback in analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple media channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Transmit ideas through all those mediums which help to build public opinion — the radio, the lecture platform, advertising, the stage, the motion picture, the mails — not only the press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select and coordinate among channels (press, radio, lectures, advertising, film, mailings, etc.) to reach target publics; match medium to message and audience characteristics for maximum effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advise on client actions as well as communications
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations counsel is becoming as much of an adviser on actions as he is the communicator of these actions to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend substantive changes to client behavior, policy, or operations when necessary to align with public expectations or to preempt reputational harm; communications alone may be insufficient or counterproductive if underlying actions are at odds with messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive social responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations consultant is ideally a constructive force in the community; the results of his work are often accelerated interest in matters of value and importance to the social, economic or political life of the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for public-interest outcomes where possible; use PR efforts to advance socially valuable causes and to enhance community understanding rather than purely self-interested spin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bidirectional interpretation: interpret public to client and client to public
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations counsel is the pleader to the public of a point of view and acts as a consultant both in interpreting the public to his client and in helping to interpret his client to the public; he helps to mould the action of his client as well as to mould public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform audience analysis and translate findings into actionable advice for clients; craft messages that accurately represent client positions while resonating with the public's frames and values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand origins and psychology of public opinion (individual→group)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public opinion is the aggregate result of individual opinions; to understand public opinion one must analyze the individual mind (its judgments, authorities, and acceptance of inherited beliefs) and how these aggregate into group opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study underlying sources of beliefs (family, school, church, leaders) and psychological tendencies (dogmatism, herd instincts) to predict receptivity and resistance; use social-psychological insights when planning persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for dogmatism and logic-proof compartments
rubrics_metrics.description: Many people form definite judgments on subjects of which they know little; minds often contain 'logic-proof compartments' where beliefs persist despite contrary evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize limits of rational argument with entrenched beliefs; avoid direct shaming or name-calling. Use strategies that respect identity and existing assumptions, or work via trusted authorities to shift opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect existing a priori judgments; shift beliefs by altering authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Before attempting to modify established beliefs, counsel must consider the a priori judgment of the public; it is seldom effective to call names or discredit beliefs directly. After examining sources of established beliefs, counsel must either discredit the old authorities or create new authorities by making articulate a mass opinion against the old belief or in favor of the new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design campaigns that replace or undermine credibility of old sources (e.g., expose flaws in old authorities) or elevate new credible voices and group leaders to legitimize change; build or mobilize mass articulation rather than attacking masses directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess malleability vs. stubbornness of public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: There is divergence as to whether the public mind is malleable or stubborn; some events show stubbornness (voters ignoring press unanimity) while other institutions can bring about definite changes (e.g., woman suffrage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze historical precedents and current conditions to judge how resistant a target public will be; tailor expectations—some publics require long-term institutional engagement, others may respond rapidly to persuasive media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study interactions and evaluate relative power of channels
rubrics_metrics.description: The public and the press (and other forces) interact; action and reaction occur continually between forces projected to the public and the public itself. Counsel must understand what these forces are and evaluate their relative powers with fair accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map media and institutional ecology (press, radio, schools, churches, movies, advertising, lecture platforms) and estimate which will best influence the target audience; anticipate interactions and feedback loops among channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor messages to media standards and audience sensibilities ('fit to print')
rubrics_metrics.description: Media have standards (e.g., 'all the news that's fit to print') and editors discriminate between what the public is entitled to know and what an individual has a right to keep private; what editors judge 'significant' determines coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn and conform to editorial selection criteria (decency, privacy, timeliness, significance); craft pitches that meet the media's notion of 'fit' and avoid material likely to be excluded on those grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use intermediaries and sponsoring groups to legitimize sensitive content
rubrics_metrics.description: When material may offend prevailing sensibilities, producers used group leaders and interested groups to support and sponsor controversial works (example: 'Damaged Goods') rather than trying to educate the public directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partner with respected organizations, advocates, or thought leaders to introduce controversial topics; use sponsorship and coalition-building to lower resistance and provide cover for sensitive messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage established points of view and authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: The influence of any force attempting to modify public opinion depends upon its success in enlisting established points of view and authorities; institutions sometimes appoint respected public figures to assure public trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and recruit credible authorities (public figures, experts, community leaders) whose endorsement will lend legitimacy; align messages with preexisting, sympathetic beliefs when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listen for audience feedback and adapt (feedback-driven strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and communicators do not project thoughts into a void; they 'listen for the echo' of their words. Action and reaction are continually going on between the press and its patrons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement monitoring to capture audience reaction (media coverage, letters, sales, social signals) and be prepared to adjust messaging, tone, or channels in response; treat communication as iterative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate media constraints such as advertiser influence and reporting limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Press reporting is often constrained by advertisers' interests, readers' tastes, decency standards, and practical difficulties in uncovering and making facts interesting; perceived censorship may be due to these factors rather than malice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame stories in ways that fit commercial and practical constraints of outlets; provide newsworthy, perceivable facts that editors can present without confronting advertiser or audience limitations.
